newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish premier declares war on bikers and pushers.
newsitem.headline: Danish premier declares war on bikers and pushers.

text.p: Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen on Tuesday pledged draconian powers for the police in their war on drug dealers and biker gangs.
In a speech at the opening of parliament he sought to calm Danes, worried by a rise in violent crime and cutbacks in social services in their hitherto safe and caring country.

"People are frightened of the motorcycle gangs which are putting the lives of ordinary people at risk with their internecine rivalry. People are terrified of violence and drugs, of open narcotics trading on the streets," he said.
"We cannot accept this, everyone must be able to live and go about their business safely in Denmark," he added.
The rival Hell's Angels and Bandidos bike gangs are fighting a bloody turf war thoughout the Nordic region with guns, bombs, grenades and anti-tank missiles.
Six people have died in two years and Danes fear that it is only a matter of time before innocent bystanders become victims of attacks, frequently in densely-populated city neighbourhoods
Rasmussen's programme for the new parliamentary session and beyond includes proposals likely to meet opposition from legislators and jurists.

One plan is for the burden of proof to be reversed in cases where drug suspects have large amounts of money. If the draft becomes law they would have to prove that the money was honestly obtained rather than have the prosecution prove otherwise.
Another would give police investigating major crimes the power to tap phones and search property without a court order.
Among other pledges seen as seeking to win votes back from opposition Liberals and Conservatives are tighter immigration laws, less interference with business and improved education.
But traditional Social Democrat voters were not forgotten in Rasmussen's advance upon the middle ground.
"We insist upon improving the quality of the welfare society...The core of the government's policy is that the weakest person may lead a life of dignity," he said.

He promised the state-financed Lutheran church more funds with which to put priests in the community to counsel the socially-disadvantaged, particularly the mentally ill who have been increasingly involved in violent incidents of late.
There would also be more daycare centres and hostels for psychiatric patients and a better support structure, he added.
"We shall not send sick people to live alone with no network or contact with others."

Neither Rasmussen's speech, nor the printed catalogue of some 200 proposed bills put a price on all the planned improvements, but the prime minister said he had not given up hope of wiping out the public sector budget deficit in 1997.
"The economy is on the right course. Not since the early 1970s have the current account surplus, public finances, inflation and unemployment as a whole been in better shape than today," he said.
"The government's target is still to balance the public sector budget by 1997, but the recent period of stagnation means that this will now be a little more difficult," he added.

He said the economic outlook abroad was looking better after a growth slowdown, while the domestic economy showed returning strength, with low inflation, the lowest central bank discount rate in 60 years and growing private consumption and investment.
